# Book III, Proposition 21

*Angles in the same segment are equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/21.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.21, with Heath's letters. Drawn for one case: the segment BAED greater than a semicircle, with F on A's and E's side of BD." width="360"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Drawn for one case: the segment BAED greater than a semicircle, with F on A's and E's side of BD.</em></p>

Let ABCD be a circle, and let the angles BAD, BED be angles in the same segment BAED;

I say that the angles BAD, BED are equal to one another.

For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken, and let it be F; let BF, FD be joined.

Now, since the angle BFD is at the centre,

and the angle BAD at the circumference,

and they have the same circumference BCD as base,

therefore the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD. [III. 20]

For the same reason

the angle BFD is also double of the angle BED;

therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop21.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop21.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted, where the Lean takes a case Euclid's figure leaves aside and where the statement already gives a step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Done by `Tacit.exists_centre`.** "For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken…" Euclid takes the centre F without a reference from Heath here. The Lean takes F from `Tacit.exists_centre`, that every circle has a centre, which no rule of System E numbers.
- **Already given.** "let BF, FD be joined." The angle BFD is named by its three points, so joining BF and FD needs no further construction in the Lean.
- **Done by `Prop20.special`.** "Now, since the angle BFD is at the centre…" Heath's reference here is III.20. With F on A's side of BD, and so on E's, the Lean cites III.20's companion `Prop20.special`, where the angle at the centre is the angle BFD itself, less than two right angles, as Euclid's is; it doubles BAD here, and BED under "For the same reason".
- **Done by `Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`.** "therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED." Euclid infers that BAD and BED are equal because both are halves of BFD. `Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq` proves that equal doubles have equal halves by ruling out either strict inequality.
- **A further case, by `Prop21.greater`.** "Therefore etc." Heath says Euclid's proof reaches only the segment greater than a semicircle (vol. 2, p. 49). For F on BD or across it from A, the Lean takes Simson's completion, which Heath gives (vol. 2, p. 50): AF is drawn through the centre to C, across BD from A and E. AC and EC cross BD within the circle, by III.2, for which Heath prints no reference, and so between B and D (`Tacit.between_of_inside_chord`, System E, Circle 1, proved after III.2). So A, E and F lie on D's side of BC and on B's side of CD (`SameSideOf.of_cross`), and Euclid's case, written for any base as `Prop21.greater`, makes BAC equal to BEC and CAD equal to CED, "by the first case"; C falls within the angles BAD and BED, which those pairs make up.

<details><summary>Before the theorem, one lemma: <code>Prop21.greater</code> (11 lines)</summary>

```lean
/-- **Euclid's case, the segment greater than a semicircle.** When the centre F lies on A's
side of BD, the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD and of the angle BED, by III.20 with
the angle BFD less than two right angles (`Prop20.special`), and halves of one angle are
equal. It is Euclid's proof below, for any base, so that Simson's completion can take it
twice, "by the first case" (Heath, vol. 2, p. 50). -/
theorem Prop21.greater {A B D E F : Point} {ABCD : Circle} (hF : Centre F ABCD)
    (hA : OnCircle A ABCD) (hB : OnCircle B ABCD) (hD : OnCircle D ABCD)
    (hE : OnCircle E ABCD) (hAE : SameSideOf A E B D) (hFA : SameSideOf F A B D) :
    ∠ B A D = ∠ B E D :=
  Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq
    ((Prop20.special hF hA hB hD hFA).symm.trans (Prop20.special hF hE hB hD (hFA.trans hAE)))
```

</details>

```lean
/-- In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another. -/
theorem Prop21 {A B D E : Point} {ABCD : Circle}
    (hA : OnCircle A ABCD) (hB : OnCircle B ABCD) (hD : OnCircle D ABCD)
    (hE : OnCircle E ABCD) (hAE : SameSideOf A E B D) :
    ∠ B A D = ∠ B E D := by
  -- Let ABCD be a circle, and let the angles BAD, BED be angles in the same segment BAED;
  -- I say that the angles BAD, BED are equal to one another.
  -- For let the centre of the circle ABCD be taken, and let it be F; let BF, FD be joined.
  obtain ⟨F, hF⟩ := exists_centre ABCD
  /- Euclid's figure has F on A's side of BD, and so on E's: the segment BAED is greater
     than a semicircle. Where F is on BD or across it from A, the semicircle and the less
     segment, Simson's completion follows "Therefore etc.". -/
  by_cases hFA : SameSideOf F A B D
  · have hFE : SameSideOf F E B D := hFA.trans hAE
    -- Now, since the angle BFD is at the centre,
    -- and the angle BAD at the circumference,
    -- and they have the same circumference BCD as base,
    -- therefore the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD. [III. 20]
    have h₁ : ∠ B F D = ∠ B A D + ∠ B A D := Prop20.special hF hA hB hD hFA
    -- For the same reason
    -- the angle BFD is also double of the angle BED;
    have h₂ : ∠ B F D = ∠ B E D + ∠ B E D := Prop20.special hF hE hB hD hFE
    -- therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED.
    exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (h₁.symm.trans h₂)
  -- Therefore etc.
  /- The segment BAED a semicircle or less than one: Simson's completion (Heath, vol. 2,
     p. 50). AF is drawn through the centre to C on the circle. F is on BD, or across it
     from A, and so C is across BD from A, and from E. -/
  · have hAF : A ≠ F := ne_of_centre_of_on hF hA
    obtain ⟨AF, hA_AF, hF_AF⟩ := Postulate1 A F hAF
    obtain ⟨C, hC, -, hCFA⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hF) hF_AF hA_AF hAF
    obtain ⟨L, hB_L, hD_L⟩ := Postulate1 B D hAE.1
    have hA_L : ¬ OnLine A L := hAE.triangle.off_line hB_L hD_L
    have hAC_L : OppositeSides A C L := by
      by_cases hF_L : OnLine F L
      · exact ⟨hA_L, fun hC_L => hA_L (on_line_of_between hCFA hC_L hF_L),
          pasch3 (between_symm hCFA) hF_L⟩
      · have hAF_L : ¬ SameSide A F L := fun hs =>
          hFA (SameSideOf.of_line hAE.1 hB_L hD_L (same_side_symm hs))
        obtain ⟨X, hX_L, hAXF⟩ := OppositeSides.exists_between ⟨hA_L, hF_L, hAF_L⟩
        have hFC : SameSide F C L := pasch2 (between_inner hAXF (between_symm hCFA)) hX_L hF_L
        exact ⟨hA_L, not_on_line_of_same_side (same_side_symm hFC),
          fun hs => hAF_L (same_side_trans (same_side_symm hs) (same_side_symm hFC))⟩
    have hAC : OppositeSidesOf A C B D := OppositeSidesOf.of_line hAE.1 hB_L hD_L hAC_L
    have hEC : OppositeSidesOf E C B D := hAE.symm.trans_opposite hAC
    have hBCD : Triangle B C D := hAC.symm.triangle.acb
    /- AC and EC cross BD at X and Y, within the circle [III. 2], and so between B and D
       (Circle 1). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hX_L, hAXC⟩ := hAC_L.exists_between
    obtain ⟨Y, hY_L, hEYC⟩ := (hEC.oppositeSides hB_L hD_L).exists_between
    have hBXD : Between B X D :=
      between_of_inside_chord hX_L hB_L hD_L (Prop2 hA hC X hAXC) hB hD hAE.1
    have hBYD : Between B Y D :=
      between_of_inside_chord hY_L hB_L hD_L (Prop2 hE hC Y hEYC) hB hD hAE.1
    /- "Therefore the segment BADC is greater than a semicircle": AC crossing BD puts A on
       D's side of BC (`SameSideOf.of_cross`), EC puts E there, and F, between C and A, is
       on A's side. So the angles BAC, BEC are equal, by Euclid's case. -/
    have hDA_BC : SameSideOf D A B C := SameSideOf.of_cross hBXD (between_symm hAXC) hBCD
    have hDE_BC : SameSideOf D E B C := SameSideOf.of_cross hBYD (between_symm hEYC) hBCD
    have hFA_BC : SameSideOf F A B C :=
      (SameSideOf.of_onRay (OnRay.of_between hCFA) hDA_BC.symm.swap).swap.trans hDA_BC
    have h₁ : ∠ B A C = ∠ B E C :=
      Prop21.greater hF hA hB hC hE (hDA_BC.symm.trans hDE_BC) hFA_BC
    /- In the same way A, E and F lie on B's side of CD, and the angles CAD, CED are
       equal. -/
    have hBA_CD : SameSideOf B A D C :=
      SameSideOf.of_cross (between_symm hBXD) (between_symm hAXC) hBCD.cba
    have hBE_CD : SameSideOf B E D C :=
      SameSideOf.of_cross (between_symm hBYD) (between_symm hEYC) hBCD.cba
    have hFA_CD : SameSideOf F A C D :=
      (SameSideOf.of_onRay (OnRay.of_between hCFA) hBA_CD.symm.swap).trans hBA_CD.swap
    have h₂ : ∠ C A D = ∠ C E D :=
      Prop21.greater hF hA hC hD hE (hBA_CD.symm.trans hBE_CD).swap hFA_CD
    /- "Therefore the whole angle BAD is equal to the whole angle BED": AC and EC fall
       within the angles BAD and BED, crossing BD between B and D. -/
    have hBAD : ∠ B A D = ∠ B A C + ∠ C A D := by
      rw [angle_add_of_between hAE.triangle hBXD,
        angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hAXC) hAE.triangle.ne₁₃,
        angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hAXC) hAE.triangle.ne₂₃]
    have hBED : ∠ B E D = ∠ B E C + ∠ C E D := by
      rw [angle_add_of_between hAE.symm.triangle hBYD,
        angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_between hEYC) hAE.symm.triangle.ne₁₃,
        angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hEYC) hAE.symm.triangle.ne₂₃]
    rw [hBAD, hBED, h₁, h₂]
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L52): **Superposition.** A hypothetical placement of a triangle on a given ray and side permits a restricted derivation of metric equalities about the figure already given. - [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (through [`Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Areas.lean#L55), [`OnRay.of_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L34), [`OppositeSides.exists_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L119) and 12 other lemmas): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (through [`Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Areas.lean#L55), [`OnRay.of_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L34), [`OppositeSides.exists_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L119) and 14 other lemmas): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42) (through [`OnRay.of_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L34), [`OppositeSides.exists_between`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L119), [`OppositeSidesOf.symm`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L87) and 13 other lemmas): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: why Euclid's proof, and ours, look as they do._

**Wherever the point is taken.** By III.20 the angle BFD at the centre is double of the angle BAD, and double of BED as well, so BAD and BED are equal, halves of one angle, by the little argument met under I.37. So the angle in a segment is the same wherever its point is taken, and that is what lets Definition III.11 call segments similar by their angles.

**Must the segment contain the centre?** Heath answers that Euclid's proof needs it: "Under the restriction that the 'angle at the centre' used in III. 20 must be less than two right angles, Euclid's proof of this proposition only applies to the case of a segment greater than a semicircle, and the case of a segment equal to or less than a semicircle has to be considered separately. The simplest proof, of many, seems to be that of Simson" (vol. 2, p. 49).

**Robert Simson makes two greater segments.** Draw AF through the centre to C, and join CE. Heath gives Simson's next step: "Therefore the segment BADC is greater than a semicircle, and the angles in it BAC, BEC are equal, by the first case" (vol. 2, p. 50). In the same way CAD is equal to CED, and the two pairs make up BAD and BED. This C is Simson's, the end of a diameter; in Euclid's figure C only names the circle.

**Euclid's case, then Simson's.** Under Euclid's sentences our proof runs his two steps where the centre F is on A's side of BD, the case his figure draws: there the angle BFD is less than two right angles, as his angles at the centre are, and III.20 doubles BAD and BED (`Prop20.special`). The semicircle and the less segment, where F is on BD or across it from A, follow his sentences by Simson's completion, with Euclid's case taken twice (`Prop21.greater`). What Simson reads off his figure, that the segment BADC is greater than a semicircle, we prove: AC and EC cross BD between B and D, which puts A and E on D's side of BC, and F, between A and C, on their side too. Our III.20 also has an angle at the centre of any size (`angleAtCentre`), with which Euclid's two steps would reach every segment; that reading is ours, not Euclid's, so this proof leaves it aside and argues each case as Euclid or Simson does.

**The modern way.** In complex numbers the angle BAD is the size of the argument of (D − A)/(B − A). So III.21 says that for A and E on one circle through B and D, on one side of BD, the cross-ratio ((D − A)/(B − A)) / ((D − E)/(B − E)) is a positive real number; four points lie on one circle or one straight line exactly when it is real.

## Further reading

- Julian Lowell Coolidge's preface to [*A Treatise on the Circle and the Sphere*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924001508955) (1916, free online), p. 3, explains why Postulate 5 lies under every fact about circumferences: had Euclid taken Lobachevsky's or Riemann's assumption instead, "he would have been unable to prove that all angles inscribed in the same circular arc are equal". This great old treatise is wholly about the circle and the sphere, scholarly but rewarding to dip into.
- For the cross-ratio of the modern way, real when four points lie on one circle, Dan Pedoe's [*Circles: A Mathematical View*](https://doi.org/10.1090/spec/012) (1995), in its section "The cross-ratio of four complex numbers" (pp. 47–49), a small, concise book given wholly to the circle, gentle in its opening Chapter 0 and more demanding later.
- The second case is "wanting in the Greek", says Robert Simson's note on III.21 (p. 366), which draws a simpler proof from the first: [*The Elements of Euclid*](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_elements-english-sele_euclid_1756_0) (1756, free online) (also on [III.1](01.md)).
